messages.subject: Re: Help on Fit statistics and contraining error variance (theta-delta)
messages.subject_clean: Help on Fit statistics and contraining error variance (theta-delta)
messages.body_plain:
On 02/29/2016 10:35 PM, tom...@rhsmith.umd.edu wrote:
> Hi, I've been trying to do an CFA on my dataset in R to replicate what
> my professor did in Lisrel (he's old-school and doesn't believe R can
> handle SEM and CFA).

The problem is the the lisrel model is not identified. The 'Perf' latent
variable gets (by default) a free variance, and a free residual variance
for its single indicator 'perform'. As a result, LISREL says:

  W_A_R_N_I_N_G: TD 13,13 may not be identified.
                 Standard Errors, T-Values, Modification Indices,
                 and Standardized Residuals cannot be computed.

Unlike lavaan, it still reports fit indices in this case.

To mimic this underidentified model in lavaan, you can use:

model <- '
      Perf =~ 0.948683*perform
      Perf ~~ NA*Perf
      perform ~~ perform
      Tnp =~ tnp1 + tnp2 + tnp3
      Con =~ conp1 + conp2 + conp3
      Snp =~ snap1 + snap2 + snap3
      Effp =~ effp1 + effp2 + effp3
'
fit <- sem(model, data = Data, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, mimic = "EQS")

To get an identified model in lavaan: remove either the second (Perf ~~
NA*Perf) or third (perform ~~ perform) line. IN LISREL: either fix the
variance of 'Perf' to unity, or fix the residual variance (in the
theta-delta matrix) to zero.

> Also another question I couldn't figure out is
> how to constrain theta-delta (error variance) in lavaan. In Lisrel you
> can do "Set the Error Covariance of perform to 18.749", for example.

To fix the residual variance of, say, 'conp2' to 18.749, you should add
a line like this:

conp2 ~~ 18.749*conp2

Hope this helps,

Yves.

I don't see any output in your post, but by default, the mean structure will be identified by setting the latent means to zero, whether std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE or FALSE (same defaults as Mplus). messages.subject: Re: FIML and Mean Structure
messages.body_plain:
FIML requires means in order to calculate the log-likelihood of each observation (for variables on which each person was observed).  Calculating subject i's multivariate normal density (likelihood) requires their vector of observations, the estimated mean vector, and the estimated covariance matrix.  You can see this in the formula for the PDF <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Density_function> and by the necessity for this information in an R function (in the mvtnorm package) that calculates multivariate density:

?mvtnorm::dmvnorm

Complete data does not require a mean structure because the formula for -2LL (chi-squared) can be simplified to using summary statistics (estimated using all variables from every observation).

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-pI1KVB3ou2Q/VtfyDLNXqQI/AAAAAAAAAB8/FZEi2tl7CCw/s1600/MLwithMeans.png>

If your mean structure is saturated (or if your have mean-centered data), then the last term falls out because the difference between x-bar and mu = a vector of zeros.  When using FIML, you can't just exclude a term when your mean structure is saturated because you need to know the mean vector of the subset of variables on which that person has observed data to calculate the multivariate normal likelihood of that vector of observations.

It's not specific to SEM, but I think the section on FIML starting on p. 18 of this article is pretty enlightening.

dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2009.10.001 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2009.10.001>

Terry

messages.body_plain:
> I am trying to run a SEM model that has a binomial endogenous variable, and want to compare whether a grouping factor increases the fit or not.  As far as I understand, these models (due to the DWLS estimator?) will not provide AIC scores, which I was planning to use to compare models.

The inclusion/exclusion of a predictor means the models are nested, so you can use a chi-squared difference test.  But your problem is that you aren't fitting the 2 models to the "same data" (at least not in the sense required to compare fit measures).  Instead of fitting one-group and multigroup models, fit them both as multigroup models.  In the first, allow all parameters to be free across groups (they will be by default, as you currently specify it), and in the second (nested) model you can constrain all parameters to equivalence across groups.  Then you can compare the models using the anova() function.

Terry

As the messages indicate, you have a Heywood case (negative variance estimate), and you can use the inspect() function to find out which parameter it is.

> When I run the same model, but without the ordered=c() part - it manages to run. What could be the problem?

Well, there's no reason to expect that fitting the model to different data (ordered vs. continuous) will yield the same results.  They can yield similar results under certain circumstances:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0029315

But you can get Heywood cases regardless of the estimator, and they can indicate either model misspecification, or perhaps just sampling error if you fit a model in which the population values happen to be close to a natural boundary.  This paper talks about testing the null hypothesis of the sampling-error explanation (but it is still worth considering whether your model is misspecified by looking at fit measures and standardized residuals):

http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138

> had some evidence for weak invariance.

invariance is the null hypothesis, so you can't have evidence in favor of it, only against it (i.e., reject or fail to reject the null), unless you use Bayesian methods to calculate a Bayes factor with the likelihood of the null in the numerator.

> "We further investigated the measurement invariance for gender following Milsap and Yun-Tein(2004). There were no evidence for strict or strong invariance but the test for weak invariance was almost insignificant

There is no "almost" significant in NHST.  Your alpha level, albeit arbitrary, is the boundary used to make a binary decision. You never know whether you've made a Type I error by rejecting (or Type II error by failing to reject) the null, but you can only know your probability of making a Type I error = alpha if you treat the alpha level like it is supposed to be treated.  (I'm not always a proponent of NHST, I'm just pointing out that we should either commit to doing NHST correctly or find another way to answer our research questions, e.g., examining impact of noninvariance on latent parameter estimates to see whether it is even worth worrying about, or using Bayes factors to compare evidence in favor of competing hypotheses).

Terry

> A final question: to make the correct comparison for my case (i.e. whether the grouping factor increases the fit of the model), should I constrain "loadings", "intercepts", "regression", or all? (although the model with the last option did not converge).

An omnibus test of equality of covariance matrices across groups would require you to constrain all parameters.   To make sure it is working correctly, I suggest counting the number of parameters in your single-group model, and making sure that's how many more degrees of freedom the constrained 2-group model has than the unconstrained 2-group model.

I think you want to use group.equal = c("regressions","residuals","intercepts"), but that might not constrain the (co)variances of your exogenous variables (fat + muscle + wing_length), assuming you want fixed.x = FALSE.  But if you want to treat exogenous means/(co)variances as known instead of random, then that's not a problem.

> Now I would like to add a moderator variable to this direct effect - demotion - which is also a latent construct.

You cannot use the asterisk in lavaan syntax to automatically calculate product terms as you would in a formula object (e.g., for lm() or glm() models).  When you have an interaction among observed predictors, you would need to calculate the product term and store it as a variable in your data set, then include that product term in your regression formula in the lavaan syntax.

But you cannot use lavaan syntax to estimate an interaction involving a latent predictor.  You can look into the nlsem package to use the latent moderated structures (LMS) approach, which Mplus implements.  Or you can look into the semTools package for helpful functions to implement the product-indicator approach in lavaan.  (Look up the ?indProd help page for details and references describing the method.)

Terry

messages.body_plain:
lavaan gives you a warning message about which matrix is nonpositive definite, and the message also tells you how to investigate it (using the inspect() function -- which has actually been superseded by the lavInspect() function).  If your lavaan object is called "fit" and the error message was about the latent variable covariance matrix, then you could inspect it like this:

lavInspect(fit, what = "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

A negative value on the diagonal would be an out-of-bounds estimated variance, making it nonpositive definite.  If the problem is a correlation being beyond +/- 1, then you can find it looking at the correlation matrix:

lavInspect(fit, what = "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>")

Look at the ?lavInspect help page to see what else you can look up.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
> what happens to "structural" missing? Of the 4927 people I start with only 1473 make it through all the waves.
>

> I mean: someone who was only there for 2 waves should not be excluded, he/she should simply not get a summary score of cognition beyond wave 2.

This is a discussion I've had before without reaching a firm conclusion, but I'll share my perspective.  Because this is not specific to lavaan, you might see what people on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> have to say.

The analysis is agnostic about these "structural missing" cases, so I think your imputation model should be specified the same way.  If you fill in best-guesses for all holes in your data (whether they are supposed to be missing or not), then the parameter estimates should not be biased by including the estimated missing values for people who "shouldn't" have observed values.  The goal of multiple imputation is not to make inferences about those imputed values; it is just to have unbiased point and SE estimates of the model parameters.  Multiple imputation is asymptotically equivalent to FIML (i.e., they give you the same answer when you use an infinite number of imputations and the imputation model matches the analysis model).  So although FIML is more aesthetically pleasing because it "handles" the missingness by ignoring it (i.e., maximizing the likelihood of available data with respect to only the associated parameters), multiple imputation should give you the same unbiased results that FIML would have (with additional Monte Carlo variance).

This analogy might make you more comfortable.  Rubin (inventor of multiple imputation) described estimation of causal effects as a missing data problem.  When we estimate the mean difference between a treatment and control group, we want to know the effect of the treatment condition.  That value would in reality be the difference between the treatment-group's response to the treatment condition and the (same) treatment-group's response to the control condition.  (Or equivalently, the difference between the control-group's response to the treatment condition and the (same) control-group's response to the control condition.)  We are missing the information about:
what the treatment group would have scored if they had been in the control group
what the control group would have scored if they had been in the treatment group
Because randomization makes the treatment and control groups statistically equivalent (on average), we use the control group's observed mean as a proxy/estimate of the missing mean of (1), and we use the treatment group's observed mean as a proxy/estimate of the missing mean of (2).  The fact that it is not possible to observe the treatment (or control) group in both the treatment and control conditions makes (1) and (2) "structural" missing values in the same sense you used it in your post.  It doesn't matter whether the unobserved cases past Wave 2 were not supposed to be measured -- you can think of the imputed values as proxies of values you might have observed in a hypothetical (even if impossible) situation (counterfactuals, in Rubin's vocabulary), and those imputed values serve no other purpose than to allow you to obtain unbiased point and SE estimates.  If your goal is to estimate factor scores (which are indeterminate, so I wouldn't recommend doing so in general), then you can calculate those estimates and simply ignore the ones it doesn't make sense to interpret.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Constraining Indirect Effects
messages.body_plain:
> 2.  From what I have read, a nested models approach is better than simply taking the  X_square difference between each group without imposing a specific equality constraint on the indirect effect of interest.

The chi-squared difference between two nested models (with and without constraint(s) ) is the only nested model approach I am familiar with.  Could you be more specific?

> 3. how do I provide different path labels for each group for the purposes of estimating indirect effects for group 2?

By using a vector of labels (one for each group) instead of a single label.  See the examples in the second half of this page:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

Using the same label for both groups (e.g., M1 ~ c(a, a)*X) will constrain that parameter to equality across groups, but using different labels (e.g., M1 ~ c(a1, a2)*X) will allow them to be free, while still allowing you to use the labels to define new parameters (i.e., indirect effects).

> I realize they can be calculated and Sobel tested for significance, but for the purposes of constraining for group comparisons, how can that be done?

Bias-corrected bootstrap CIs control Type I error rates better than Sobel test.

> 4. Assuming #3 can be addressed, how would I constrain, say, ind1 across both groups? I've seen a little bit about this in MPlus discussion, but I'm lost here.

Indirectly (pun intended), but constraining each of the associated direct effects to equality across groups.  I don't think it would make sense to constrain only the product to be equal because the direct effects might differ while coincidentally yielding the same product (e.g., 0.2*0.3 in Group 1 vs. 0.4*0.15 in Group 2).

> 5. Assuming #3 cannot be addressed in lavaan, is it acceptable for me to just make the comparison between the two models?  Is there a manual calculation for determining significant differences between indirect effects without first performing the nested model comparison overall?

OK, that test would make sense, insofar as comparing the size of the indirect effect across groups.  When you use different labels for Groups 1 and 2, then you define different a different indirect effect in each group.  You can then define a difference parameter and look at the BC-Boostrap CI for that.

> ind1 := a1*b1          # group-1 indirect effect
> ind2 := a2*b2          # group-2 indirect effect
> indDiff := ind1 - ind2 # group difference

The likelihood-ratio test (i.e., chi-squared difference test between nested models) tends to be the most powerful test available, so you might prefer it to testing the 95% CI for the group-difference parameter.  And although there is nothing preventing you from constraining

> ind1 == ind2

in your syntax and conducting a chi-squared difference test, I think it would be more prudent instead to constrain the direct effects to equality by using the same labels and calculating a single indirect effect, then comparing that constrained model with the unconstrained model.

> 6. Necessary disclosure: I did run a nested model comparison with which I compared the freely estimated group model with another constrained model where a and c (and consequently their indirect coefficient) were both constrained  to be equal

You don't want to test whether the 2 different direct effects are equal within a group.  You want to test whether each of the same direct effects are equal across groups.

>  PROCESS analysis in SPSS that actually includes the dichotomous IV suggests that these differences are there.

Using the grouping variable as a predictor does not allow the residual variances to differ across groups.  If you have heteroscedasticity (a testable assumption), then the estimated sampling variance will be biased.  I'm not sure bootstrapping the indirect effect entirely overcomes this -- perhaps it depends how the bootstrapping is performed.  But I would put more trust in the multiple-group approach, unless your sample sizes are small.

Terry

You can do either or both, depending on which research question you want to answer.  The model equalmeans is nested within fitEqualLV1, which is nested within scalarinva.  So could even put all three in the anova() function, or a pair at a time.  In either case, you are testing the null hypothesis that the constraints in the more-constrainted model (with more df) hold in the population.  So

> anova(scalarinva, fitEqualLV1)

tests the null hypothesis that the second and third means are equal across groups.  By contrast,

> anova(equalmeans, fitEqualLV1)

already assumes those means are equal (because the constraint exists in both models), so you are testing the null hypothesis that the first mean is equal across groups.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone! I am new to this community and am interested in using lavaan as my primary SEM software. One of the aspects of lavaan that appeals to me is that unlike closed source solutions in which we have no way real way of verifying that the different estimation procedures are mistake free or have been implemented correctly, it is possible to verify in lavaan.  As someone who is interested in better understanding SEM/CFA and contributing to SEM methodological research in the future, I believe the open source nature of lavaan is extremely attractive.

With that said, I am a SEM (and R) novice and thought that lavaan (or perhaps a more basic SEM package in R) might help be better understand how SEM models are estimated. I want to again, emphasize that I am a beginner so I apologize if some of this seems really obvious to everyone here!

Specifically, I would like to compare how different estimators function (i.e. ULS, WLS, DWLS) and to connect the equations and more general explanations I have found elsewhere to an actual coded implementation of those estimators.

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/discrep.html#refs

Is there a good way to digest the code in smaller pieces or get started? For instance, using the CFA example from the website I thought I could step through the model using debugonce(lavaan) and obtain some insight but I didn't get out what I expected (probably wishful thinking here). I think I naively half expected to have to step through a loop with some kind of optimizer (e.g., Newton Raphson) that continued until it reached some convergence criteria (in the case of the ULS estimator 39 steps). For me, watching one of these iterative optimization procedures for any one of these estimators (ULS, WLS, DWLS, ML) would be very helpful.

Here is the example model I was referring to.

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

Debug(lavaan)

# fit the model

fit <- cfa(HS.model, estimator='uls', data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

I did a lot of searching through the different functions (when I say function I'm just referring to pages within the overall larger lavaan github e.g., lavaan/R/lav_samplestats.R, or  lav_fit_measures) within the lavaan program on github also and I think what is confusing is that I don't know what many of the variables correspond to (although they seem informative!).

I'm not looking for anything comprehensive here of course, but I would very much appreciate any tips

(e.g. "you don't understand how R functions are written so what youre saying doesn't make sense…so you should know X, Y, and Z", or "you should 'step-through' an old version of the lavaan program which might be easier to read because we had less features at the time" )

regarding how I can better approach the source code and thereby hopefully get a better understanding of how SEM is implemented in practice. Thanks everyone!

Jordan

P.S. I didn’t find any kind of discussion similar to this anywhere else in the google group so I'm sorry if I missed something.

> I wish to compute polychoric correlations between 17 items using lavCor. I am able to get the following results but I am also getting error messages. Can the results be trusted given the error messages?

Those are not error messages.  Those are just warnings, letting you know that you have empty cells in some bivariate tables, so the estimates of tetrachoric correlations were estimated by replacing those zeros with 0.5 (see the zero.add argument in the ?lavaan help page).  If you want more information, this article discusses the difficulty of estimating polychorics with empty cells and evaluated some correction methods:

http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10705511.2011.557339

Judging from her conclusions, you can probably trust your estimates because her recommendations are lavaan's defaults for zero.add.

Terry

> (a) Lavaan gives both "Variances:" and "Scales y*:" for the endogenous variables. In my case, the values are 1 in both cases for both Y1 and Y2. Is that possible?

You expect the default delta parameterization to return Scales of y* == 1 (with residual Variances == 1 - explained variance), or theta parameterization to return residual Variances == 1 (with Scales of y* == 1 + explained variance).  The reason you do not see this is because the default is "fixed.x = TRUE", so the variances of the predictors are not model parameters.  Hence, there is no way to estimate the "explained variance" component in the above equations.  You will get the expected behavior if you set the argument sem(..., fixed.x = FALSE)

> (b) I get the following error. Can you point to the literature that explains this error
> Warning message:
> In muthen1984(Data = X[[g]], ov.names = ov.names[[g]], ov.types = ov.types,  :
>   lavaan WARNING: trouble inverting W matrix; used generalized inverse

It is not an error. It is a warning.  You are using weighted least squares, and the weight matrix couldn't be inverted, so it used a generalized inverse (you can read about it on Wikipedia, or Wolfram Alpha under "Moore-Penrose matrix inverse").  I don't know if this means you can't trust your results.  I assume neither does the developer -- that's why it's just a warning.

> (c) I modified my model to make it non-recursive by adding Y1 as an explanatory variable.
> model2 <- '
> Y1 ~ x1+x2
> Y2 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + Y1
> Y1 ~~ Y2
> '

That is still a recursive model.  It is a very common mediation model (well, common with continuous variables).  If this is actually a model from which you are interested in interpreting indirect effects, have a look at the caveats for mediation with categorical variables in these slides (starting with slide 22).

http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf

If you just wanted to make a non-recursive model for the fun of it, you can add a feedback loop (e.g., also have Y2 predict Y1, or have either Y predict any of the Xs).

Good question.  I am surprised that lavaan proceeds to fit a model to NPD matrices -- although perhaps that is necessary to allow models to be fit when there are missing ordered data and we want to use pairwise deletion (which might yield a NPD polychoric matrix).

The SEs just mean that the information matrix can be inverted.  But it does seem suspicious that lavaan found a perfectly fitting solution, so I used your example data & model, and I found something curious:

> covMat <- structure(c(1, 0.81170673, 0.81170673, 0.81170673, 0.37068154,
>                       0.04348156, 0.8117067, 1, 0.8117067, 0.8117067, 0.3706815, 0.1989328,
>                       0.8117067, 0.8117067, 1, 0.8117067, 0.3706815, 0.3558707, 0.8117067,
>                       0.8117067, 0.8117067, 1, 0.3706815, 0.8844411, 0.3706815, 0.3706815,
>                       0.3706815, 0.3706815, 1, 0.16, 0.04348156, 0.19893281, 0.35587069,
>                       0.88444112, 0.16, 1), .Dim = c(6L, 6L),
>                     .Dimnames = list(c("m1","m2","m3","m4","Y","X"),
>                                      c("m1","m2","m3","m4","Y","X")))

> LVMod <- 'LM =~ m1 + m2 + m3 + m4

>           Y ~ LM
>           LM ~ X'
> fitLV <- sem(model = LVMod, sample.cov = covMat, sample.nobs = 100,
                  sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)

The observed (S) and model-implied (Sigma) covariance matrices DO differ, so the solution should not be perfectly fitting.

> > (S <- lavInspect(fitLV, "sampstat")$cov)

>    m1    m2    m3    m4    Y     X

> m1 1.000
> m2 0.812 1.000
> m3 0.812 0.812 1.000
> m4 0.812 0.812 0.812 1.000
> Y  0.371 0.371 0.371 0.371 1.000
> X  0.043 0.199 0.356 0.884 0.160 1.000
> > (Sigma <- lavInspect(fitLV, "sigma.hat"))

>    m1    m2    m3    m4    Y     X

> m1 0.797
> m2 0.509 0.797
> m3 0.503 0.515 0.773
> m4 0.612 0.628 0.620 0.718
> Y  0.209 0.214 0.211 0.257 0.735
> X  0.680 0.697 0.688 0.838 0.286 1.000

Because S cannot be inverted, it has a negative determinant, and log(det(S)) == NaN, so that should mean fmin == NaN.  But because X is treated as a fixed exogenous variable by default, its variance and covariances are not estimated parameters, so fmin is not calculated from the 6x6 matrix.  I assume it is calculated from the 5x5 submatrix (excluding row/column X), which as it turns out, is positive definite:

> > fS <- S[-6,-6]
> > fSigma <- Sigma[-6,-6]
> > det(fS)
> [1] 0.01926308

So it would be possible to calculate fmin from the reduced matrices.  But I don't that is what lavaan does because that quantity is also not zero:

> > log(det(fSigma)) - log(det(fS)) + sum(diag(fS %*% solve(fSigma))) - nrow(fS)
> [1] 1.42241

I am unsure exactly how fmin is calculated in the presence of fixed exogenous variables, but even after setting "fixed.x = FALSE" (in which case I would expect fmin == NaN because log(det(S)) == NaN), lavaan still returned fmin == 0.  So I am curious what Yves has to say about this situation.

messages.body_plain:
The bootstrapLavaan() function only returns the bootstrap distribution of the statistic(s), so I don't think you can get the bias-corrected CI this way.  You can get it using the boot function (from the boot package that comes with R by default).  For example:
>
> ## Define a function that fits a model to your data and returns the
> ## Std. estimates. The boot function requires the first argument to
> ## be the data.frame, and the second argument to be an index to
> ## select rows (i.e., to do bootstrap sampling)
> getSTDs <- function(data, rowIndices) {
>   library(lavaan)
>   mySyntax <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>                 textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
>                 speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
>   fit <- cfa(mySyntax, data = data[rowIndices, ] )
>   standardizedSolution(fit)$est
> }
>
> ## run bootstrap
> out.boot <- boot(data = HolzingerSwineford1939, statistic = getSTDs, R = 2000)
>
> ## get bias-corrected CI, for one parameter (index) at a time
> boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(out.boot, type = "bca", index = 1)
>
> ## note the index corresponds to the actual order in which
> ## the parameters appear in the output:
> example(cfa)
> standardizedSolution(fit)
>
> ## You can request a set of BCa CIs
> lapply(1:3, function(x) boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(out.boot, type = "bca", index = x))

You need a lot more than 100 bootstrap samples to get a stable bias-corrected CI -- try 2000-5000.  You can use boot's built-in parallel options to make it go faster:

> out.boot <- boot(data = HolzingerSwineford1939, statistic = getSTDs, R = 2000,
>                  parallel = "snow", ncpus = parallel::detectCores() - 1)

If you just want bias-corrected CIs for raw parameters, you can get those using the arguments in the lavaan() and parameterEstimates() functions

> fit <- lavaan(mySyntax, myData, ..., bootstrap = 1000L)
> parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "bca.simple")

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Jon,
I agree that this is more of a SEMNET question than a lavaan question.

I think that what is happening is this.  You have saturated the covariances among indicators of the same LV with correlated residuals.  So, the factor model parameters are identified by the covariances between indicators of different LVs.  This is similar to a bifactor model in which each LV is like a general factor and the correlated residuals are like orthogonal specific factors with two indicators each.  The linear relationship between the LVs may not suffice to account for the pattern of covariances between indicators of different LVs.

A good place to start might be Bollen & Diamantopoulos (2015) followed by Edwards (2011).  You might also find chapters 6-8 of my book with Denny Borsboom helpful.

Once you arrive at a model that makes sense for your purposes, if something like this comes up, the matrix of correlation residuals can be very helpful in working out the problem areas in a model.  This is especially helpful in tandem with consideration of the constraints that the model places on the moment matrix.  Personally, I like to put the non-redundant residuals into a stem-and-leaf plot to evaluate outliers.  If you have a large number of saturated covariances, sometimes it can be helpful to filter out the zero residuals first.

>>>
sessionInfo()
require(lavaan)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)

# Extract residuals
implied_cov <- inspect(fit, "cov.ov")
observed_cov <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov
implied_cor <- cov2cor(implied_cov)
observed_cor <- cov2cor(observed_cov)
residuals_cor <- observed_cor - implied_cor
residuals_cor

# Plot residuals
residuals_cor_unique <-
  residuals_cor[lower.tri(residuals_cor, diag=TRUE)]
stem(residuals_cor_unique)

# Plot non-zero residuals
residuals_cor_unique_nonzero <-
  residuals_cor_unique[residuals_cor_unique != 0]
stem(residuals_cor_unique_nonzero)
>>>

Good luck,
Keith

> >
> > ## run bootstrap
> > out.boot <- boot(data = HolzingerSwineford1939, statistic = getSTDs, R = 2000)
> >
> > ## get bias-corrected CI, for one parameter (index) at a time
> > boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(out.boot, type = "bca", index = 1)
> >
> > ## note the index corresponds to the actual order in which
> > ## the parameters appear in the output:
> > example(cfa)
> > standardizedSolution(fit)
> >
> > ## You can request a set of BCa CIs

>

>
> > fit <- lavaan(mySyntax, myData, ..., bootstrap = 1000L)

>

I'm guessing this is an artifact of not giving the optimizer anything to do.  That is, you aren't actually estimating anything if all the parameters are fixed.  I suppose Mplus might  have programmed a check for such a case, where they skip the optimizer and just use the fixed parameters as the final solution, and perhaps Yves hasn't included such a check. > Sigma <- fitted(fit1)$cov
> S <- cov(d)
> ChiSq <- log(det(Sigma)) - log(det(S)) + sum(diag(S %*% solve(Sigma))) - nrow(S)

Then you can look up formulas to calculate any other ChiSq-based indices you want.  For CFI/TLI, you can grab the ChiSq of the baseline model from another lavaan object where you actually have estimates (or just fit your own baseline model).  Bollen's SRMR is pretty easy to calculate:

> corResiduals <- diag(diag(solve(S))) %*% resid(fit1)$cov %*% diag(diag(solve(S)))
> mean(lav_matrix_vech(corResiduals))

On 03/15/2016 09:18 AM, Jordan wrote:
> With that said, I am a SEM (and R) novice and thought that lavaan (or
> perhaps a more basic SEM package in R) might help be better understand
> how SEM models are estimated.

The best way to learn it, is to program it yourself. Really. To get you
started, I will paste below some code that uses some lavaan at the
beginning (to set up the list of model matrices in MLIST), and to get
some starting values, but apart from that, it is plain R. And we will
fit the three-factor CFA model, using two different estimators: GLS and
ML. Other estimators are easy to add. lavaan is nothing more but a
slightly more fancy shell around this bare-bones code.

Hope this helps,

Yves.

# bare bones code to fit the 3-factor Holzinger & Swineford CFA model
# manually (YR 25 march 2016)

library(lavaan)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "GLS") # or ML

# initial list of model matrices
MLIST <- lavTech(fit, "start")

# sample covariance matrix
S     <- fit@SampleStats@cov[[1]]

# inverse and logdet of S
cS <- chol(S)
S.inv <- chol2inv(cS)
diag.cS <- diag(cS)
S.logdet <- sum(log(diag.cS * diag.cS))

# x is the parameter vector: fill in new values in the model matrices
x2MLIST <- function(x, MLIST) {
     lambda.x <- x[1:6]; theta.x <- x[7:15]
      psi.x <- x[ c(16,19,20,19,17,21,20,21, 18) ]

     MLIST$lambda[ c(2,  3, 14, 15, 26, 27) ]            <- lambda.x
     MLIST$theta[ c(1, 11, 21, 31, 41, 51, 61, 71, 81) ] <- theta.x
     MLIST$psi[ c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) ]           <- psi.x

     MLIST
}

# objective function 'GLS'
objective_GLS <- function(x, MLIST) {

     MLIST <- x2MLIST(x = x, MLIST = MLIST)

     # compute Sigma.hat
     Sigma <- lavaan:::computeSigmaHat.LISREL(MLIST = MLIST)

     # GLS
     R <- (S - Sigma)
     A <- R %*% S.inv
     objective <- 0.5 * sum(diag(A %*% A))
     cat("objective = ", objective, "\n")

     objective
}

# objective function 'ML'
objective_ML <- function(x, MLIST) {

     MLIST <- x2MLIST(x = x, MLIST = MLIST)

     # compute Sigma.hat
     Sigma <- lavaan:::computeSigmaHat.LISREL(MLIST = MLIST)
     nvar <- NROW(Sigma)

     # ML
     cS <- chol(Sigma)
     Sigma.inv <- chol2inv(cS)
     diag.cS <- diag(cS)
     logdet <- sum(log(diag.cS * diag.cS))
     objective <- logdet + sum(diag(S %*% Sigma.inv)) - S.logdet - nvar
     cat("objective = ", objective, "\n")

     objective
}

# get starting values
start.x <- parTable(fit)$start[ parTable(fit)$free > 0 ]

# estimate parameters GLS
out.GLS <- nlminb(start = start.x, objective = objective_GLS,
                   MLIST = MLIST)
out.GLS
# chi-square
out.GLS$objective * 301
# 77.72896

# estimate parameters ML
out.ML  <- nlminb(start = start.x, objective = objective_ML,
                   MLIST = MLIST)
out.ML
# chi-square
out.ML$objective * 301
# 85.30551

messages.body_plain:
Why are you regressing the slope on the intercept?  Typically, the intercept and slope are just allowed to freely covary, then you can regress both the intercept and slope on Condition.  Also, you are fitting a very constrained model: the mean increases after Time 0, but then stays exactly the same.  The only thing you are allowing to differ between conditions is the initial status and how much the mean changes between Times 0 and 1.  Have you plotted your observed means in each group to see how tenable this assumption is?

You have a substantial sample size, so you might considered fitting a 2-group model instead of using Condition as a predictor.  You can test for main and interaction effects by labeling intercept and slope means in each group, and try constraining them to equality.  But you would also be able to relax the homogeneity of (Level-1) residual variances across groups.

I don't know if any of that explains why you are getting some missing SEs, but if they still occur, you might need to post enough data to reproduce the problem.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
> Our prediction is that there should be only a change between time 0 and 1 and after that no change. That's why I would like to investigate the option of a stepwise regression.

You said that in your first post.  I asked why you were regressing an intercept on a slope.  Does your theory also say that someone's rate of change is caused by their initial status?

> Your suggestion of testing for main and interaction effects is really interesting. Can you say a few more words about what you mean by " labeling intercept and slope means in each group, and try constraining them to equality". How can I relax the homogeneity of (Level-1) residual variances across groups?

There are details about labeling parameters and making across-groups constraints in the lavaan tutorial on multiple groups

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

If you understand what you are modeling, then you know the effect of condition on the latent intercept estimates how much the average initial status differs between groups (i.e., a simple effect of condition on "level" at Time 0), and the effect of condition on the latent slope estimates how much the slope (i.e., the effect of Time) differs between groups (i.e., an interaction between Time and Condition).  In a multiple-group model with no constraints across groups, you don't estimate those parameters explicitly, but you allow the intercept and slope to differ across groups, so you are implicitly allowing for a simple effect of Condition on the Intercept and on the Slope.  You can test whether those parameters significantly differ using nested models (chi-squared difference test) by constraining the Intercept mean to equality and seeing if the fit is significantly worse.  If not, then you can additionally constrain the Slope mean and test whether fit is significantly worse (i.e., is there an interaction, or do slopes differ between groups?).

Terry

> 1. In our dataset, each person has a unique time score for each wave- depending on when they answered the survey. I have created a variable to represent these unique scores. Is there a way to use this variable as the growth parameter so that each person has a unique score? (In MPLUS this is done with the TSCORES command.)

Unfortunately, I don't think this is possible in lavaan, and I'm not sure whether there are plans to allow individuals to have different fixed parameters in future versions.  You can do so in the OpenMx program (its flexibility makes it less user-friendly and intuitive, but it may be worth learning if you need this kind of flexibility).

You could also do so using Bayesian software.  If you have not used BUGS, JAGS, or Stan before, the blavaan packages would be a way to write your model using lavaan syntax, then it would be translated into a JAGS script for you.  You could then replace the fixed loadings for the latent slope with variable loadings, which you would have to supply as data.  This option is also not trivial, but it may be worth learning if you want this kind of flexibility using open-source software.

Actually, you could even go directly to the optimizer that lavaan uses.  Yves recently provided a useful example for a user to see how the lavaan engine works (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/0Hitqi3k_do/SGKNNH8pAQAJ).  You might be able to adapt the functions in this example to use a list of lambdas (one unique lambda vector per person) as data instead of a fixed lambda matrix as parameters.  I doubt it would be any easier than the above two options, but if you can learn to use one of R's built-in optimizers, you might never need to rely on anyone else's software again :-)

Good luck,

messages.subject: Re: Modelling Method Factors
messages.body_plain:
I would only recommend the error-covariances approach when you only have a few items per method (3 or less), because that is statistically equivalent to actually modeling the method factor(s), in the sense that you estimate as many parameters and get the same model-implied covariance matrix.  In your case, you have several items to measure each method factor, so I would recommend actually modeling the method factors, using a much more parsimonious bifactor model:

> Model <-  '
> Factor =~ GENAT_1 + GENAT_2 + GENAT_3 + GENAT_4 + GENAT_5 + GENAT_6 + GENAT_7 + GENAT_8 +
>           GENAT_9_R + GENAT_10_R + GENAT_11_R + GENAT_12_R +
>           GENAT_13_R + GENAT_14_R + GENAT_15_R + GENAT_16_R

> Pos =~ GENAT_1 + GENAT_2 + GENAT_3 + GENAT_4 + GENAT_5 + GENAT_6 + GENAT_7 + GENAT_8
> Neg =~ GENAT_9_R + GENAT_10_R + GENAT_11_R + GENAT_12_R +

>        GENAT_13_R + GENAT_14_R + GENAT_15_R + GENAT_16_R

> Factor ~~ 0*Pos + 0*Neg
> '

If you are unfamiliar with bifactor models, it is pretty easy to Google around for basic information about them and find references.  For instance, you might also need to constrain the Pos~~Neg covariance to zero if there are still identification issues, although I'm pretty sure you can estimate it (and expect it to be negative).  But method factors should be uncorrelated with general/trait factors.  You can also search the SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> archive for more discussions about bifactor models and MMTM modes, since this isn't a lavaan-specific issue.

Terry

x.names <- lavNames(lavaanify(model1), "ov.x")

2) create the 'X' matrix:

X <- analysisdata[,x.names]

X1 <- as.matrix(X[complete.cases(X),])

XX <- crossprod(X1)

chol(XX)

[1] "DLAge"

Removing this variable makes XX invertible.

Yves.
